jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e106.summary: Editorial title of the single question for distinction 44 of book II (Wadding edition): whether the power of sinning comes from God.

jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e113.summary: Editorial list of parallel loci (Aquinas, Bonaventure, Richard of Middleton, Durand, Biel) for the question, placing it within the commentary tradition on Sentences II d.44.

jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e122.summary: Scotus states the question for the last distinction of book II and gives the argument for the negative from Anselm's De libertate arbitrii: being able to sin is neither freedom nor a part of freedom, so the fact that free choice comes from God does not make the power to sin come from God, and it comes from him in no other way.
claims: According to Anselm, the ability to sin is neither freedom nor part of freedom.
Hence God's giving free choice does not mean he gives the power to sin.

jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e147.summary: Argument for the opposite: Peter Lombard, in the text of the distinction, cites authorities including Romans 13, that there is no power except from God; so the power to sin, being a power, is from God.
claims: There is no power except from God (Romans 13).
So the power to sin is from God.

jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e165.summary: Heading marking the start of the editor's scholium, an editorial aid distinct from Scotus's text.

jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e170.summary: The editor's scholium summarizes the resolution: taken as something absolute, the power of sinning is from God, because it is the will itself; the same holds if it is taken as a relation to the substrate of sin; but taken as a relation to what is formal in sin, it is not from God, since the formal element of sin is nothing.
claims: As an absolute, the power to sin is the will and is from God.
As a relation to the act underlying sin, it is from God.
As a relation to sin's formal deformity, it is not from God, because that deformity is nothing.

jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e186.summary: Scotus's reply opens with a distinction that structures the answer: 'power of sinning' can mean either the immediate ordering (relation) to the act of sinning, or the foundation of that ordering, by which its possessor is called able to sin.
claims: 'Power of sinning' can signify either a relation to the act of sinning or the foundation of that relation.

jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e202.summary: First branch of the distinction, the power as relation. If the relation is to the act that underlies the deformity, it is from God, as both its terms are, and God himself has power over that underlying act since he causes it (not only the created will does, on one opinion). If the relation is to the deformity itself, it is nothing, as its term (sinning, formally taken) is nothing, and so it is not from God.
claims: The relation to the positive act underlying sin is from God, who also causes that act.
The relation to the deformity of sin is nothing, since sinning formally is nothing.
What is nothing is not from God.

jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e236.summary: Second branch, the power as foundation. Something positive grounds the relation in both senses. Just as in passive powers one subject receives both a habit and its privation, so a free, defectible active power is the immediate subject of opposites: by acting it produces rectitude, by failing it produces sin. This absolute power is properly a power for both, effectively for the one and defectively for the other. In this sense the power of sinning is from God: it is the nature by which one is able to sin, not by effecting but by failing, and this positive nature is the proximate ground of that failing.
claims: A positive reality is the foundation of the power to sin.
A free defectible active power is the immediate subject of both acting rightly and failing.
It is a power for rectitude effectively and for sin defectively.
Taken as this foundation, the power of sinning is from God.

jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e288.summary: Objection and reply: one might say the will fails only because it comes from nothing, not because of anything positive in it. Scotus answers that being defectible in the sense of being able to lapse into nothing belongs to every creature as made from nothing, but being defectible by sinning is proper to this kind of nature and follows from its specific character as a principle of opposites, able both to act and to fail.
claims: Every creature is defectible in that it can lapse into non-being, being made from nothing.
Defectibility by sinning is proper to the will's specific nature as a principle of opposites.

jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e319.summary: Reply to Anselm: freedom absolutely is a pure perfection (perfectio simpliciter) and is formally in God; in us it is limited. Its formal ratio can be considered without the limitation, as wisdom can. Our will thus includes freedom, a pure perfection, together with a limitation that is not a pure perfection. The ability to sin, and the proximate foundation of the ordering to actually failing, belong to the will by reason of the limitation, not by reason of freedom as such.
claims: Freedom absolutely taken is a pure perfection and is formally in God.
Created freedom combines a pure perfection with a limitation.
The ability to sin belongs to the created will because of its limitation, not because of freedom itself.

jdso8u-d1e2352-d1e382.summary: How Anselm should be read: being able to sin is nothing of freedom taken as a pure perfection, which is all his argument from its absence in God proves. Taken as created freedom with its ordering, the ordering to sin is still not part of it; but as the proximate foundation of that ordering, the power to sin is part of it. Since that power is a positive being, it is from God, from whom, through whom and in whom are all things. The doxology ends book II.
claims: Anselm's claim holds for freedom as a pure perfection.
As the proximate foundation of the ordering to sin, the power to sin belongs to created freedom.
As a positive being, the power to sin is from God.

jdso8u-d1e2352.summary: Ordinatio II d.44, single question and the close of book II (Wadding edition, with editorial title, parallel loci and scholium): whether the power of sinning is from God. Against Anselm's claim that being able to sin is no part of freedom, and with Romans 13, Scotus distinguishes the power as a relation from its foundation. As a relation to the positive act underlying sin it is from God; as a relation to sin's deformity it is nothing and not from God. As foundation it is something positive: the free, defectible will, which is the subject of opposites, causing rectitude effectively and sin defectively; so taken, it is from God. Its defectibility by sin is specific to the will's nature, not just the general defectibility of creatures made from nothing. Anselm is reconciled by distinguishing freedom as a pure perfection, which does not include ability to sin, from created freedom, whose limitation grounds that ability.
claims: The power of sinning, taken as a positive foundation (the free, defectible will), is from God.
The relation to sin's formal deformity is nothing and is not from God.
The created will causes rectitude effectively and sin defectively.
Ability to sin follows from the limitation of created freedom, not from freedom as a pure perfection.
